results.narration: Something below Kenny’s flat was thumping too hard and smelling of scorched plastic. In the laundrette downstairs, a dryer was smoking—and no one was shouting, running, or trying to stop it. Kenny heard no bus, no neighbour, no shouting. Warehouse nights had taught him bad machines, so he pulled on the steel-toe boots by his bed, grabbed his torch and gloves, and went down. The laundrette was bright and empty. Washers churned, the dryer smoked, and shoes, coats, a handbag and a buzzing phone lay scattered across the tiles. Smoke thickened, so he found the back utility cupboard. He had helped the owner before, so he knew the breaker and stopcock. The machines died into emergency-lit dripping silence. He tried the counter phone, then his mobile. Recorded voices looped, hold music played, and no operator or siren came. So he crossed to the public bench with the clear view and waited. For ten stubborn minutes, shop alarms blinked, a bus idled, café coats sat ownerless, and nobody appeared. Then smoke alarms screamed down the road. Kenny understood the city was full of machines working alone, so he went upstairs to pack.

results.narration:
Stranded on a stopped ski lift after closing, your rescue begins when your signal fails. The ski you drop becomes the one thing the groomer can’t ignore. At dusk, you take the small hill’s last chair, alone, in a white jacket, orange neck gaiter, rental skis, poles, gloves, and a phone at nine percent. Halfway up, the chair jolts, swings, and stops. You shout toward the bottom terminal, but the lift shack goes dark.

Your phone shows no service, so you save it and search below. A groomer starts across the lower run. You flash and yell when it turns, but its engine swallows your voice, its lights slide behind trees, and the phone dies.

The cold sharpens, so you unclip one ski, tie your gaiter to it with a pole strap, and swing the reflective barcode stickers beneath you. The strap slips through your glove. The ski falls into the groomed lane and slides into the headlights.

The groomer brakes, lights lifting to your chair. Soon patrol inches you to the top, and you one-ski into the patrol room, blanketed, while the radio reports your ski down on the lane.

After lifts close, grooming machines begin working the lower runs, but their drivers are focused on the snow in front of them, not the chairs overhead.
Night temperatures drop quickly; staying still on an exposed chair becomes dangerous within hours.
Cell service on this part of the hill is unreliable, especially below the ridgeline.

results.narration:
Every morning, your car looks a few inches closer to the wooden bench beside it. The doors stay locked, but a black crescent on the bumper lines up with one rubber bench leg. In the apartment lot, phone and keys out, you know you parked farther away. Scrape trails lie under it, and the service sign says deliveries use this entrance before five.

That evening, you park carefully, photograph it, outline the tires and bench legs with chalk from your move, then take one wide photo from the kitchen window.

In the morning, the tire outlines match, but the bench outline is broken. It sits crooked near the bumper, so your suspicion flips. The car is staying put.

Before dawn, you leave the kitchen light off and watch from the window. Just after four, a delivery worker arrives with stacked crates, drags the bench aside to wedge the service door open, then shoves it back by foot while steering the cart. The rubber leg taps the crescent mark and stops inches off.

You show the supervisor the photos. Next morning, taped lines hold the bench away, and your car is unchanged.

beats.heroWants: You want the nightly bumping to stop without turning a small discovery into a fight.

beats.heroWants: You want proof that the explanation was right and that the pattern is over.
beats.heroKnows: You know the cause, the time it happens, and the simple fix.
beats.state: You are in the lot the following morning, holding your keys, looking at the car and the taped bench position.

resolution.what: The car was not being secretly driven; the bench beside it was being dragged for predawn deliveries and reset badly, changing the reference point and bumping the bumper. Once the bench is marked and moved away from the car, the morning difference stops.

You accidentally text your boss, “He manages like an alarm clock with a LinkedIn account.” To survive, you claim it’s for a comedy sketch—so he books you to perform it at Friday all-hands.

Minutes earlier, Darren orders the deck redone for vague reasons, so everyone leaves furious. In the break room, Jae expects your rant. Beside you are Friday’s comedy-slot flyer and Darren’s process survey. You send the line, then see Darren’s name. Delivered.

You try unsend but he replies, Was that meant for me?

Because you wrote he not Darren, you call it sketch material. Darren wants to look approachable, so he says it is funny and makes you opener.

At your desk, Jae helps soften it until Darren posts the original in team chat. Reactions pile up because everyone recognizes the redo.

Friday arrives and the room laughs until Darren asks who the alarm clock is.

You admit it came from frustration over the redo, which is what his survey was meant to catch. Darren sees the team agreeing, cancels the redo, and asks for process notes. You keep your job but the insult becomes homework.

worldRules.rule: This is an ordinary workplace with ordinary messaging: once a text is delivered, you cannot depend on pulling it back from the recipient’s phone.

beats.cause: You are frustrated from the meeting and texting on autopilot to the person you usually vent to.
beats.heroWants: Undo the text before Darren sees it.

You are awake at your bedroom window, phone in hand. The house is empty, power kept on for viewings, but it stands close to yours, with dry bins and a wooden fence between. results.narration:
When Kenny woke, there was a voicemail in his own voice, left while he’d been asleep: “Do not open the front door. Window. Bench.” His phone buzzed on the floor. Muted after his shift, it had missed forty-seven calls, all from his own number.

Above the laundrette, boots and keys by the bed, Kenny hated nonsense, but warehouse work had trained him to notice heat, smells, wrong sounds. He tested the front door without opening it.

The handle was warm. Brown smoke pressed under the frame.

“Fine,” he said. “Window.”

At the window, below the laundrette sign, sat the ugly bolted bench he passed every morning. The painted sash stuck, so he grabbed a steel-toe boot and smashed the lower pane.

Glass toothed the frame. Kenny pocketed the phone, dropped the boot, climbed out with both hands, lowered onto the sign, and fell onto the bench. His palm bled. Smoke burned his throat.

Then his pocket rang.

His own number.

He answered. His own voice said, “Move.”

Kenny stepped off as the upper frame gave way. Burning glass crashed onto the bench. He stood in dawn street, bleeding, one boot short.

candidates.text: The voicemail was in Kenny’s voice, but Kenny had been asleep when it was left. It said, “Do not open the front door. Window. Bench.”
candidates.promise: Kenny is receiving instructions from an impossible version of himself, and those instructions will have to be tested.
candidates.paidOffIn: B2 pays it off when the front door is warm and smoke is under the frame; B3–B5 pay off “Window. Bench” as his escape route.

candidates.text: Kenny nearly opened his flat door before he felt the heat in the handle. Smoke was already pressing under the frame.
candidates.promise: Kenny is trapped in a burning building and must escape without using the obvious exit.
candidates.paidOffIn: B2 confirms the stairwell is unsafe, and B3–B5 deliver the escape through the window, onto the laundrette sign, and down to the bench.

candidates.text: Kenny had one normal way out of his flat, and the voice on his phone told him not to use it. He listened just long enough to stay alive.
candidates.promise: A single choice—trusting or ignoring the impossible call—will decide whether Kenny survives.
candidates.paidOffIn: B2 shows that opening the door would be deadly, B5 shows him surviving by following the window-and-bench instruction, and B6 shows him obeying the second warning in time.

candidates.text: The safest thing in Kenny’s flat was a broken window. The front door was already too hot to touch.
candidates.promise: The story will flip the normal escape route: the door is danger, and the window becomes survival.
candidates.paidOffIn: B2 makes the door unsafe with heat and smoke; B4 opens the stuck window with the steel-toe boot; B5 gets Kenny outside through that broken window.

reviews.note: Instantly understandable and raises the impossible-call mystery, but it delays the life-or-death instruction that makes the calls urgent.
The impossible voice, the fact Kenny was asleep, and the exact warning are all clear and concrete. The plot directly pays off the door, window, and bench instructions.
A clean survival opening, but it leaves out the story’s most distinctive hook: Kenny being warned by his own voice.
Good focus on the survival choice, and the plot pays it off, but the wording is broader and less vivid than the voicemail version.
A punchy reversal of normal escape logic, but it starts with the fire mechanics rather than the impossible calls that drive the story.

pick.hook: When Kenny woke, there was a voicemail in his own voice, left while he’d been asleep: “Do not open the front door. Window. Bench.”
pick.promise: Kenny will have to decide whether to trust an impossible warning from himself, and the specific words in the voicemail will become the key to escaping alive.

plotPick.reason: Plot 0 is the stronger short narrated video. It gives the viewer one urgent situation, one easy-to-track question, and a complete earned outcome inside the episode: Kenny survives because he tests, then trusts, the impossible calls. Every setup pays off visibly, and the mystery remains as a hook without withholding the main satisfaction. Plot 1 is clever and coherent, but it is more of a setup for a larger mystery than a fully gripping 75-second story.
plotPick.rejected: The stakes are softer for most of the episode; Kenny is curious rather than endangered until the final warning. In 75 seconds, the search procedure may feel more procedural than emotional. Finding an identical phone explains the call source but raises so many bigger questions that the 'resolution' may feel less satisfying than the escape plot. The final warning depends on delayed danger rather than the danger being visible now.
